name: Hair length for face shape (long hair maxxing)

lead: Matching hair length, shape and parting to your face, or growing hair longer under labels such as long hair maxxing, frames your features and makes the jaw and forehead look more balanced.

Proponents say length and volume change perceived width and jaw outline through visual framing. Encyclopedic sources say stylists weigh face and head shape, hair type and the wearer's desired image. No published study has tested specific lengths for rated attractiveness.

paras: People try a stylist's recommendation or grow hair out over months, adjusting layers, parting and volume to the face. Growing out takes time, and styling products help it hold shape.
Low risk overall. Dermatology guidance links tight braids, extensions and dreadlocks to traction alopecia, and bleaching or dyeing has been linked in some research to health risks.

web.title: The Hairstyles That Make You Look Most Intelligent And Attractive (PsyBlog)

chain: Jaw and forehead look more balanced
angle.text: Matching hair length and shape to your face, or growing it out, frames your features and makes the jaw and forehead look more balanced. The change in outline is visible as the hair grows or is styled.

lead: Choosing hair length to suit the shape of the face, and growing hair longer to frame or soften facial features, is a style practice discussed in appearance-focused communities under labels such as "long hair maxxing". The idea is that length, volume and parting change how the outline of the face, jaw and forehead are perceived, so a well-matched cut can make the same face look more balanced, with a stronger jaw or a shorter-looking forehead.

Encyclopedic sources describe hairstyle choice as depending on several factors, including the wearer's face and head shape from various angles, overall body proportions, natural hair type and growth pattern, and the wearer's desired self-image.[1] Looksmax.org has threads in which users ask which haircuts suit a given face shape, such as a diamond face, and respondents answer that the choice depends on hair type, suggesting medium lengths or a mod cut.[2]

Hair length carries social meaning. Long hair on men has signalled wealth in ancient Greece, a countercultural statement in the 1960s, and is widely accepted today in part through the man bun trend.[3] A survey led by psychologist Marianne LaFrance, commissioned by a hair-care brand, found perceptions varied by style, with medium-length side-parted male hair rated as looking intelligent and short front-flipped hair rated sexiest.[4] No published trial has tested whether a particular hair length improves rated facial attractiveness for a given face shape.
infobox: Growing or choosing hair length to frame the face
Perception surveys; no face-shape trials found

paras: Practitioners generally group faces into shapes (for example round, oval, square, diamond or long) and match cut length, layering and parting to them. Longer hair is said by proponents to add width or soften angles, while shorter styles are said to expose the jawline. These categories are folk typologies used in styling advice rather than a standardized guide.[1]

Hair length has carried social meaning across cultures and eras. In most societies men's and women's hair have differed, and in Western societies long hair is strongly associated with femininity, although long hair was common among both men and women in the 1960s and 1970s.[1] In early modern Europe men's hair lengthened in the early 1600s and wigs became fashionable, before short, neoclassical styles spread in the late 1700s.[1]

Wikipedia's article on long hair adds that in ancient Greece long hair signalled wealth and power, short military cuts became standard after World War I, and the 1960s made longer hair on men a countercultural statement popularised in part by the Beatles. Today shoulder-length or longer hair is widely accepted for men, partly because of the man bun trend.[3]

On looksmax.org, face-shape haircut threads typically ask for named cuts. In one, a user with a diamond face asks for options besides a low taper with a fringe, and respondents say the answer depends on hair type and suggest a medium length or a 'mod cut'.[2]

A PsyBlog summary of a survey led by Marianne LaFrance, commissioned by a hair-care brand, reports that participants rated photos of the same man with different haircuts on personality scales. Medium-length side-parted hair looked intelligent, short front-flipped hair was rated sexiest, shorter highlighted hair looked confident, and long hair was linked to good nature but lower intelligence; medium-length centre-parted hair did not noticeably affect ratings. The summary does not state the sample size or control for face shape.[4]

The American Academy of Dermatology categorized hairstyling practices by alopecia risk in 2016, linking tight braiding, extensions and dreadlocks to traction alopecia and advising looser styles.[1] Some research cited in the same overview associates bleaching and dyeing with higher risk of certain cancers, while long dark hair may offer some UV protection.[1]
No studies found of hair length matched to face shape. A commissioned perception survey of haircuts is described above.[4]

lore.intro: Face-shape haircut advice is a staple of looksmaxxing style threads, where users ask for specific cuts for their shape.[2]
